Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Romanian real estate developer One United Properties, listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange, said that it recorded residential transactions worth EUR 106.1 million in the first half of 2026, covering 229 residential and commercial units. The average contracted selling price reached EUR 3,853 per sqm, up 24% year-on-year. The transactions, which included sales, pre-sales, and reservations, covered a total surface area of 25,221 sqm, alongside 396 parking and storage spaces. One Floreasca Sunset was the company's best-selling development during the period, with around 73% of its residential and commercial units reserved since sales began at the end of March. “Buyers today are more selective, and when a development offers the right location, product and long-term value, demand remains strong,” said Victor Căpitanu, co-CEO of One United Properties. As of June 30, 75% of the units in the company's developments under construction had been contracted, with 1,002 units still available for sale. Another 158 units were available across completed residential projects. One United Properties plans further residential launches during 2026, including One City Club, One Cotroceni Towers, and One Park Lane in Bucharest, as well as One Riverfront in Sibiu. The company said contracted cash collections reached EUR 445 million at the end of June, scheduled through 2029. Of this amount, EUR 150 million is expected in 2026, EUR 165 million in 2027, EUR 85 million in 2028, and EUR 45 million in 2029. “While the new legislative framework has altered the timing of customer payments, it has not changed the fundamentals of our business," said Andrei Diaconescu, co-CEO of One United Properties. The developer started handing over units at One Floreasca Towers and One High District, with additional projects expected to be completed later this year. Meanwhile, headline rent from its commercial portfolio reached EUR 14.7 million in the first half, up 3% compared with the same period of 2025. The company leased and pre-leased 5,000 sqm of office and retail space during the period. At the end of June, One United Properties' standing commercial portfolio comprised almost 152,000 sqm of gross leasable area and was 95% leased. Including One Technology District and One Gallery, both fully pre-leased ahead of delivery, the portfolio reached almost 195,000 sqm, with an overall lease and pre-lease rate of 96%. One United Properties had 3,939 residential units and 45,500 sqm of office and commercial space under construction at the end of the first half, representing a total gross development value of EUR 1.53 billion. Its landbank comprised 538,900 sqm of land, with development rights for 1.34 million sqm above ground. The company estimates the portfolio could accommodate approximately 11,000 residential units and 106,000 sqm of commercial buildings, with a gross development value of EUR 2.7 billion. irina.marica@romania-insider.com (Photo source: press release) Read next 28 July 2026 Real Estate British investor Ghai Sant Ram acquires plot near Bucharest for new residential project Normal Real Estate One United Properties reports EUR 106 mln in residential transactions in H1 2026 05 August 2026 Irina Marica Like this article? https://metro.co.uk/2026/09/16/microphon.text: The cables will turn the ocean floor into a ‘continuous array of microphones’ (Picture: BAE Systems) You can’t see them from space, but a network of critical undersea cables powers the UK. The wires and pipelines carry over 90% of the nation’s daily internet traffic and are worth £65bn to the economy. The race is on to protect these lifelines, which are currently ‘naked’ and ‘incredibly vulnerable’ to sabotage from Russia and other states. Metro can reveal that undersea microphones are being developed to give the British military a leg up in this future battleground and help shield the UK from devastating attacks on its cables. Experts at defence firm BAE Systems are developing these vibration-detecting sensors for military use, which will attach to cables and catch oncoming threats. Thousands of kilometres of vital undersea cables run out of the UK (Picture: Parliament.uk) Cables have long been at risk of accidental disruption, such as when ships unwittingly drag their anchor, or when fishermen trawl the seabed. But now there is little doubt that Putin and other hostile states have their eyes on this critical undersea infrastructure (CUI). Just last week, Nato forces foiled a Russian subsea sabotage plot, when they chased away ships in Arctic waters training to attack the cables with an undisclosed secret weapon. Then Defence Secretary John Healey warned in Parliament last year that Russia was ‘gathering intelligence and mapping’ the UK’s cable network. ‘Much of our life as we know it goes through cables,’ says Tim O’Neill, Subsea Intelligence lead at BAE Systems. ‘There has been a real increase in the threat to this undersea infrastructure. It is no longer just benign accidents.’ Researchers at the defence giant are now working on a way to turn this very vulnerability into a military asset for the UK. The answer lies in attaching powerful sensors onto the fibre optic cables. Known as distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), the technology can detect even the faintest of vibrations near the cable, affecting the fibres. BAE Systems want to revolutionise how these DAS sensors are used so they can ‘turn a cable running for hundreds of kilometres alongthe ocean floor into a continuous array of microphones’. The sensors would be able to detect any vibration on the seabed near the cable, and identify ‘everything from environmental shifts to the movement of vessels and even marine life’. The microphones will able to detect vibrations on the seabed – here is the take of Metro’s cartoonist Guy Venables (Picture: Guy Venables) The sensors are already used widely on land but also on a limited commercial basis under the water. But BAE want to advance this technology for military purposes. O’Neill explained how it could work: ‘You will get an alert that something has hit the seabed at this position on the cable. ‘DAS will be able to pick up that anchor dragging far enough away that you can tell the vessel to stop, or if that doesn’t work, you still have time to send out military assets to intercept it.’ The tech is currently in its experimentation phase, with data being fed from a DAS sensor on a cable into BAE’s AI and machine learning programmes. ‘The reality is that this is a state problem,’ O’Neill added. ‘If we can get this into the hands of the UK government to support their activity, trying to counter Russian threats, then we want to be part of that.’ The challenge for experts is not just making sure the tech works, but figuring out how to handle the reams of data it pumps out. That’s because BAE estimates that a single DAS unit can generate up to a petabyte of data per day, which is the equivalent of streaming 57 continuous years of high-definition video. So tools are also being developed which will tools which will identify the signals of interest as they appear and alert the operator. Undersea cables have been described as ‘naked’ and ‘incredibly vulnerable’ (Picture: Getty Images) Defence experts believe the new undersea microphones could mark a ‘small revolution’ in the future of underwater battle. Alessio Patalano, who specialises in critical undersea infrastructure King’s College’s War Studies Department, believes the data from the sensors will enable military chiefs to better defend the ‘incredibly vulnerable’ cables. He said: ‘The sensors provide persistent and consistent data on how to understand what’s happening around the cable in a way that was impossible. ‘It makes the seabed slightly more transparent, making it easier to understand where to operate, how to operate, and against whom you are operating. ‘It will also improve the ability to recover from any interference with the cables, because you are going to be faster at identifying where the problem is and the best way to address it.’ The Ministry of Defence has been approached for comment.
